opus-5.5.text:
I think coding has been one of the most striking areas of progress, and it's probably the clearest signal of where these models are heading.

A few years ago, models could autocomplete a line or write a small function, which was impressive but limited. Now they can work in a real repository: read lots of files, figure out how the system is structured, make changes across modules, run tests, look at the failures, and iterate. That's a qualitative shift. It's moved from "writing code" to something closer to "doing software engineering."

Part of why coding moved so fast is that it's an unusually good environment for training. You have verifiable feedback: code compiles or it doesn't, tests pass or they fail. That makes reinforcement learning much more effective than in fuzzier domains. Coding is also a kind of universal interface. If a model can write and run code, it can use tools, manipulate data, and act in a digital environment, so progress here spills over into agents more broadly.

But I'd be careful about how we read the benchmarks. Solving a well-specified issue with a test attached is very different from what a senior engineer actually does. Much of real engineering is deciding what to build, understanding vague requirements, making trade-offs about maintainability, and working with other people over months. Models are getting much better at execution, but long-horizon judgment, understanding context that isn't written down, and knowing when to ask instead of guess are still hard.

So my view is that we've gone from AI as a tool you call to AI as a collaborator you delegate to, and the frontier now is how long and how independently it can work before a human needs to step in. That horizon is getting longer quickly. I think the interesting questions over the next few years are less about whether models can write correct code and more about how we design the collaboration: how humans specify intent, review work, and stay in the loop as the model takes on bigger chunks of the job.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier line or small-function completion with current work across repository files and modules. It does not clearly identify a prior tendency to focus on one file while overlooking relationships among files, so the specific core condition is only partially conveyed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the progress has been genuinely remarkable, and in some ways it's the clearest case study we have for how AI capabilities actually move.

If you look back to around 2022, 2023, the way we measured coding ability was mostly things like HumanEval — you give the model a function signature and a docstring, it writes a few lines, you run some unit tests. That's a very self-contained problem. Models got good at that quickly, and honestly the benchmark saturated. But solving a LeetCode-style function is very different from what a real software engineer does.

That's partly why we built SWE-bench. The idea was: take real GitHub issues from real repositories, give the model the codebase and the issue description, and ask it to produce a patch that makes the failing tests pass. When we first released it, the best models were solving something like one or two percent of the problems. It was humbling. The model could write a nice function, but it couldn't navigate a codebase, figure out which files mattered, understand the existing abstractions, and make a change that fit.

And then within a fairly short period, the numbers went from low single digits to a majority of problems solved. I think that jump tells you something important. It wasn't only that the base models got smarter — it's that the models learned to act as agents. They learned to read files, run tests, see the error, go back and fix it. The loop of thinking, acting, observing — which is basically what ReAct was pointing at — turned out to be the thing that unlocked real software engineering, not just better code generation in a single shot.

So where are we now? I'd say the models are genuinely useful for a large fraction of day-to-day engineering work — bug fixes, well-specified features, refactoring, writing tests. Lots of engineers now have an agent in the loop for most of their work. That's not hype; that's just how people are working.

But I'd also be careful not to overstate it. What's still hard is the stuff that isn't well specified. Real engineering is often about deciding what to build, understanding why a system was designed a certain way, making tradeoffs across a long time horizon, coordinating with other people. The benchmark problems have a clear success signal — tests pass or they don't. A lot of real work doesn't. And the models still struggle when the task spans a very long horizon, when the feedback is delayed or ambiguous, or when the environment is messy in ways the training distribution didn't cover.

So my view is: the first half of this problem — can a model write correct code in a real codebase — is largely solved, or on a clear trajectory to being solved. The second half is about environments and evaluation. How do we define the tasks that actually matter, and how do we get the right reward signal for them? I think that's where the interesting work is now, and it's less about model architecture and more about carefully designing what we ask the model to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes models improving at navigating codebases and identifying relevant files, but it does not identify a reduced tendency to focus on one file while overlooking relationships across files.

astra-6.text:
I think the progress is substantial, but we should distinguish generating code from doing software engineering. If you give a model a well-defined problem and a way to check the answer, it can already be very useful. It can write an implementation, run tests, and revise its approach based on the results.

Real software engineering is less clearly specified. You need to understand an existing codebase, figure out what the user actually wants, and make a change that works with everything else. Sometimes the difficult part is discovering which problem you should solve, rather than writing the code itself.

So I see two dimensions of progress. One is the model’s ability to understand and generate code. The other is its ability to act in an environment—to inspect files, use tools, interpret failures, and keep working toward a goal. Those capabilities reinforce each other, because software provides relatively concrete feedback.

The remaining question is reliability over longer tasks. A model can make several good decisions and then make one mistaken assumption that sends it in the wrong direction. Getting it to recognize that, recover, and verify the final result is a big part of moving from a useful coding assistant to something that can independently handle software-engineering work.

r001.rationale: The response says software engineering requires understanding an existing codebase and making changes that work with everything else, but it does not identify a recent substantial reduction in models’ tendency to focus on one file while missing cross-file relationships.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the progress is substantial, but we need to distinguish writing code from doing software engineering. Models have become much better at turning a clear specification into a function, fixing a localized bug, or adding tests. When the task is well defined and you can quickly check whether the result works, they can be very useful.

But in a real codebase, often the hardest part is figuring out what the task actually is. Which files matter? What assumptions does the existing system make? Is this change going to break something elsewhere? You have to explore, run tests, interpret failures, and revise your approach. Generating the code is one part of that process.

So I see the next stage as moving from a model that answers a coding question to an agent that can work through that whole loop. And reliability is crucial. If it produces something plausible, but a person has to inspect every step and repeatedly rescue it, that limits how much work you can delegate. The interesting question is increasingly: how much of a real engineering task can it complete independently, and how confidently can we verify the result?

r001.rationale: The response says real engineering requires understanding which files matter and whether a change breaks something elsewhere, but it does not identify a recent, substantial reduction in models’ tendency to focus on one file and overlook cross-file relationships.
